counterexample.verified_how: Exhaustive exact-arithmetic census of all 1,338,193,159,771 unlabeled order-14 posets, each certified against Peczarski's Gold Partition criteria; no counterexample to the conjecture was found (the census result confirms the conjecture holds at this order, it does not refute anything).

summary: Two lines of activity touch this problem's own quantity (the balance constant delta(P)) since the frozen revision, neither of which resolves the general conjecture. (1) Max Aires and Jeff Kahn, in two 2025 preprints (arXiv:2509.11549, Sept 2025, and arXiv:2510.26134, Oct 2025), prove new asymptotic lower bounds on delta(P) for posets of large width (delta(P) -> 1/2 as n -> infinity under width/minimal-element conditions, delta(P) >= 1/e - o(1) under weaker width conditions) and study a related Kahn-Saks variance question for bounded-width posets. I fetched both abstracts directly; neither paper mentions the 1/3-2/3 conjecture by name in the fetched abstract content, and I found no statement of AI involvement in either paper's abstract or from search results on their acknowledgements. These are asymptotic bound improvements on the conjecture's own constant for a restricted class (large/bounded width), so they are genuine cases/progress under Section 3.1, but they leave the general conjecture (which needs delta(P) >= 1/3 for ALL non-chain posets, including small-width, bounded-size ones near the known worst cases) untouched, so status does not move to partial/resolved from these alone. (2) A July 2026 solo preprint by independent researcher Anish Gupta (arXiv:2607.23926, v1 2026-07-27, v2 2026-07-30) reports an exhaustive computer census of all order-14 posets (1,338,193,159,771 isomorphism classes, 4,096-way sharded exact-integer computation), verifying Peczarski's Gold Partition Conjecture -- which implies the 1/3-2/3 conjecture -- through n=14, one order beyond the prior exhaustive frontier of n=13 (De Loof, De Baets, De Meyer 2010) and n=11 (Peczarski 2006). This is a genuine case of the universally-quantified conjecture (restricting to posets of size <=14), so it counts under Section 3.1, and it is the event the status rests on. However, it is a single-author preprint with no journal acceptance, no traced expert digestion (no MathOverflow thread, no blog commentary, no citing follow-up found), so per Section 6.1 it is `claimed` rather than `resolved`, notwithstanding the exact-arithmetic, no-floating-point, independently-recomputed-witness design that makes the computation itself easy to check. Crucially, the paper's own text states plainly that 'Anthropic Claude Code (Claude 5 family) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.6 family) were used extensively for software development and optimization, computational experiment design, literature discovery, and drafting and editing the manuscript' -- an explicit, first-person authorial disclosure, which is the required basis for an ai_role other than none. I classified this as assisted rather than none because 'computational experiment design' plausibly extends beyond mechanical coding/proofreading into the design of the verification approach itself (which sharding scheme, which independent-recomputation cross-checks to run), which is part of the mathematical/algorithmic content of the result, not merely code cleanup. Wikipedia's live article (checked for context, not as a substitute for primary sources) already cites this exact preprint for the '14 elements' claim, confirming the triage's find was on point.
competing_reading: A stricter reading of ai_role would put this at none rather than assisted: the quoted acknowledgement bundles 'computational experiment design' together with mundane items (software development/optimization, literature discovery, drafting/editing), and it is possible the phrase means only that the AI suggested which computations to run or helped script experiments -- i.e., an accelerant for human-directed work -- rather than that it originated any part of the mathematical argument that appears in the paper (the Gold Partition certificates, the recurrence, the sharding correctness argument). Under Section 6.2's test ('what did the model produce that appears in the final result?'), if the answer is that the census algorithm, certificates, and recurrences were all human-designed and the AI only helped implement/optimize/debug them and write prose, the correct code is none, with formalisation_only false (since this isn't formalisation, it's an empirical census). I did not find a more granular breakdown (e.g., a per-contribution list) that would let me disambiguate assisted from none with confidence; I lean assisted because 'computational experiment design' is a mathematical-methodology phrase, not a coding phrase, but this is a judgment call.
what_would_settle_it: The full paper text (methods/acknowledgements section, not just the abstract-page fetch) or the GitHub repository's commit history/documentation would show concretely which specific components (the sharding scheme, the independent witness-recomputation cross-check, the certificate logic itself) were AI-suggested versus human-designed, which would settle assisted vs. none. Separately, any MathOverflow/Peczarski/Kahn commentary on arXiv:2607.23926, or a published/refereed version, would let this move from claimed to resolved. For the general (all n) conjecture, only a full proof or an explicit counterexample at some finite n would change the status further.

corrections.why: SCOPE: `claimed` counted this among resolutions, but the record's own first sentence is 'The general 1/3-2/3 conjecture remains open'. The claimed event, Gupta's exhaustive census of posets on at most 14 elements, checks finitely many instances of a statement about all finite posets: one more example of a universal claim, which the Collatz correction (verification to 2^71) established is not movement. What remains is Aires-Kahn's asymptotic lower bounds on delta(P) for large- or bounded-width posets, a bound on the conjecture's own quantity for a restricted class, which is `progress` under 6.1. The research rules fold 'how much was settled' and 'has an expert checked it' into one field, and the agent read an unreviewed result as `claimed`; that is the pattern this batch of corrections fixes.
